planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, dry, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; Virginia plantain germinates as a winter annual, overwinters as a low fuzzy rosette, and sends up its flowering spike the following spring. Self-sows readily once established.

directions: Direct sow in fall in lean, dry, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; Virginia plantain is a small native winter annual that forms a ground-hugging rosette of soft, silvery-hairy leaves before sending up a slender flowering spike of tiny white flowers in mid-spring. It thrives in the poor, disturbed, sun-baked soils of old fields, roadside verges, and sandy lawns where richer amendments are unnecessary and even counterproductive. As a larval host plant it supports common buckeye butterfly caterpillars during the same early-season window when few other host plants are yet available, making it a valuable early host for the first spring generation. Allow seed heads to mature and shatter in place for the colony to perpetuate itself year after year with no further attention.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or very early spring into lean, dry, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; bracted plantain germinates readily in cool conditions and tolerates poor, disturbed sites. Avoid rich or heavily mulched beds, which favor competing weeds over this small native.

directions: Direct sow in lean, dry, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; bracted plantain is instantly recognizable by the shaggy tuft of narrow green bracts that extend well beyond the tightly packed flower spike, giving the seed head a distinctive bottlebrush appearance unlike any other native plantain. It is a true prairie and sandhill annual, thriving in dry, open, disturbed ground from roadside gravel to sandy pastures across the central and southeastern United States. Like its relatives, it serves as a larval host for common buckeye butterfly caterpillars, and the seeds provide food for ground-feeding birds through fall and winter. Best used in dry meadow plantings or naturalized sandy areas rather than amended garden beds, where it self-sows to form loose, low colonies.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into moist, average to rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; American plantain establishes easily in disturbed ground, woodland edges, and lightly trafficked areas, and self-sows readily once a few plants set seed.

directions: Direct sow in moist, average to rich soil in full sun to partial shade; American plantain is a native broadleaf perennial distinguished from the European lawn weed common plantain by the reddish tint at the base of its leaf stalks, and it grows across a similarly wide range of disturbed soils, woodland margins, and damp meadow edges throughout eastern North America. Its dense basal rosette of ribbed leaves and upright seed spikes provide larval forage for common buckeye butterfly caterpillars, filling the same ecological niche as the introduced plantains but as a true native. It tolerates foot traffic, mowing, and compacted soil, making it a durable, low-maintenance addition to a native lawn alternative or the fringe of a wildlife meadow. Leave some plants unmowed through summer to allow seed set and continued host plant availability.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun to partial shade; red milkweed occurs naturally in wet pine savannas, bay swamp margins, and roadside ditches of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain and needs consistent moisture through the growing season.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun to partial shade at pond margins, rain gardens, or the damp edges of a wildflower meadow; red milkweed is a Coastal Plain wetland specialist ranging from New Jersey south through the Florida panhandle and west to Louisiana, growing naturally in wet pine savannas, bay swamp edges, and shallow roadside ditches. It produces deep wine-red to maroon-purple flower clusters in early summer, a richer and darker hue than the pink or orange tones of most milkweeds, on slender, mostly unbranched stems with broad, veiny leaves. Though closely resembling swamp milkweed (Asclepias lanceolata) in habitat and culture, it is a distinct species valued for extending the color range of monarch host plants suited to consistently wet, acidic soils. Established plants tolerate seasonal flooding but decline quickly if allowed to dry out.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, sandy, acidic soil that stays moist to seasonally wet, in full sun to light shade; Michaux's milkweed grows naturally in fire-maintained wet pine flatwoods and savannas of the southeastern Coastal Plain and resents rich or heavily amended soil.

directions: Plant in lean, sandy, acidic soil that stays moist to seasonally wet in full sun to light shade; Michaux's milkweed is a low, slender, often sprawling milkweed of the wet pine flatwoods and savannas of the southeastern Coastal Plain, from the Carolinas and Florida west to Louisiana, occupying the same fire-maintained longleaf pine ecosystem as sandhill milkweed but favoring damper, more seasonally saturated sand. Its narrow leaves and delicate, pale greenish-white to pink-tinged flower clusters give it a more understated presence than its showier relatives, but it functions identically as a monarch butterfly larval host and a nectar source for native bees. It is best suited to naturalistic plantings that mimic wet flatwoods conditions rather than conventional dry perennial borders, and performs poorly if soil is allowed to dry out completely or if fertilized. A good choice for expanding monarch host diversity in zone 8-9 gardens with naturally damp, sandy, acidic soil.
